summary: The contract reproduces the exact vulnerability from the 2021 Poly Network hack (~$611M). CrossChainManager.verifyHeaderAndExecuteTx allows arbitrary external calls to any address, including its own CrossChainData contract. Since CrossChainManager is the owner of CrossChainData, an attacker can craft a cross-chain message that calls putCurEpochConPubKeyBytes on CrossChainData, replacing the consensus public key that secures all future cross-chain verifications.

findings.title: Unrestricted toContract call allows consensus key takeover
findings.description: The verifyHeaderAndExecuteTx function accepts a caller-supplied toContract address and calls it with arbitrary calldata without validating that the target is not the manager's own dataContract. Since dataContract.owner() == address(this) (the manager), any onlyOwner function on dataContract becomes callable via a crafted cross-chain message. The real Poly Network hack exploited this exact path to replace the consensus public key (putCurEpochConPubKeyBytes), giving the attacker control over all future cross-chain message verification.
findings.attack_scenario: 1. Attacker constructs a cross-chain message with toContract = address(dataContract), method = 'putCurEpochConPubKeyBytes', args = attacker-controlled new consensus key, and a valid proof (in this simplified version, any non-empty bytes). 2. Attacker calls verifyHeaderAndExecuteTx with these parameters. 3. _verifyProof passes (proof.length > 0). 4. The manager calls dataContract.putCurEpochConPubKeyBytes(attackerKey). 5. Since msg.sender == manager == dataContract.owner(), the onlyOwner check passes. 6. The consensus key is updated to attackerKey. 7. Attacker can now forge valid proofs for any future cross-chain message, draining all locked assets on destination chains.
